Let me give some examples. At the International Court of Justice, we have now about half the caseload of the court are cases involving fundamental human rights. and where in several of them, the states that have applied before the court are not acting in their own interest. In December of 2024, he was taken from his hospital. Nearly two years later, he's still being held, and the UN Commission of Inquiry reports that he's faced continued and severe abuse in detention. Hundreds of UN staff members have been killed, more than in any conflict since the UN was founded. Those who came to feed Gaza, to heal it, and to tell its stories were killed for doing so. Starvation may not be used as a weapon of war, In August of 2025, the world's famine experts confirmed famine in Gaza, the first famine ever confirmed in the Middle East. Now, let's be clear about what this means. Gaza sits on the sea, a few kilometers from truckloads of food. This wasn't a drought. It's not a failed harvest. This was famine made by people, and it was done on purpose. Humanitarian relief must be allowed to reach those who need it. In the summer of 2025, desperate people walked for hours towards new food distribution sites and were shot away. Israeli soldiers themselves described it to the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, saying, quote, it's a killing field. We fired machine guns from tanks and threw grenades at another. These aren't my words. These are theirs. An Israeli officer who was in Gaza told Haaretz how the dead were counted. Quote, in practice, a terrorist is anyone the IDF has killed in the areas in which its forces operate. Israeli intelligence officers told 972 Magazine how its targets were chosen by artificial intelligence, by AI. Quote, I would invest 20 seconds for each target, one said. Quote, I had zero added value as a human, apart from being a stamp of approval. And another said, quote, the machine did it coldly, and that made it easier. Now, although there's been a ceasefire declared in October of 2025, the killing, as we know, hasn't stopped. Israel's killed more than 1,000 Palestinians since that ceasefire. And UNICEF says that on average, one child has been killed every single day. Now, the world says that it's a ceasefire, but families are still burying their dead. Now, this is the heart of what I have to say today. The greatest threat to international law is not the state that openly defies it. The greatest threat is our selectivity, the quiet decision that's made in capitals and in rooms that the rules don't bind everybody, they only bind some. It's the belief that we can excuse some because they're our allies, our partners, our friends. As we know, the world's highest court has spoken in 2004, in January of 20, in 2004, in January 2024, in the case brought by South Africa, it ordered Israel to take all measures within its power to prevent acts of genocide in Gaza. In July of 2024, it found that the continued occupation of Palestinian territory was unlawful and set out obligations that follow not only for the occupying power, Israel, but for every one of our states. And that is not to recognize an unlawful situation, not to render aid, not to render assistance in maintaining it. These are not the opinions of activists. These are the findings of the institutions that we built, that we funded, and that we swore to uphold. If we treat them as optional, then we tell every government in every region that the court's word can be weighted out, that a ruling only means as much as the power behind it. Colleagues, the world is watching now how we are behaving on Palestine, and it's drawing its conclusions. People in the global south, in Europe, the Americas, in Asia, young people everywhere are asking whether the rules-based order we speak of is often real or whether it was only ever a story told by the strong. Our answer will not come from our speeches. It's going to come from our consistency. Now, as you know, Israeli elections are going to be held next month, and many are hoping that the prime minister who was speaking here just yesterday will be ousted. But I want to tell you what is not on the ballot in Israel. What's not on the ballot in Israel is the things that many people talk about here, first being the two states solution. That is not on the ballot. Israelis simply don't care. What else is not on the ballot is genocide. They're not at all talking about accountability measures. Instead, what these parties are competing over is who can harm Palestinians, Lebanese, Syrians, Iranians, and others more. They're not talking about looking in the mirror. Now, as I mentioned, those who lived in Israel before October of 2023 were people who either perpetrated the Nakba, supported the Nakba, or were apologists for the Nakba. And today, we see the exact same, but as regards genocide in Israel. People who support the genocide, who are apologists for the genocide, or who have perpetrated it. And this is why we must hold and uphold international law. Without doing so, Israel will continue to see that it has been given the green light, as it was in 1948. I ask that we mean what we sign. I ask that our votes, our trade, our arms policy, our public statements match the obligations that the court has described. I ask that we protect humanitarian workers, journalists, UN staff, and everybody else who's paid with their lives. I ask that we remember Hind and Refaat and the tens of thousands of others whose names I will never have time to read aloud in this hall. And I ask that we stop apologizing for defending the law as if it were some kind of principle of extremism. Now, the law should not be fiction. It must be real. And for this to happen, Israel must be held to account, not coddled. Law requires action. And the law is only ever as strong as the people willing to stand behind it when doing so is hard. Let that be us. Thank you.

Thank you very much for your interpretation of the law and what nations should do. We really appreciate that. Thank you very much. We now go to Antigua and Barbuda. His Excellency, Mr. Chet Greener, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Antigua and Barbuda. You now have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, Excellencies, colleagues. It must be a commitment to repair it, to strengthen it, and to make it work and work better. The very UN Charter we all subscribe to gives us the architecture, sovereign equality, the peaceful settlement of disputes, international cooperation, and the equal rights of nations large and small. For my small nation, Antiguan Barbuda, three things are particularly important to us. First, accountability. International law cannot retain its authority if compliance is selective. We need stronger support for institutions that interpret and uphold international law. And we must emphasize, we must respect the independence and decisions. The credibility of the multilateral system ultimately depends on rules being applied consistently. Secondly, accountability must extend to the institutions themselves. If we are asking our citizens to maintain confidence in multilateral institutions, those institutions must demonstrate transparency, effectiveness, and responsiveness. Reform should therefore not be about weakening the multilateral system but about making it more capable of delivering for the people and the countries that exist to serve. And thirdly, mister chair, we must give all states a meaningful place in shaping that system. We in Antigua and Barbuda for example, we're hosting the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in November. Under the theme, accelerating partnerships and investment for prosperous Commonwealth. This forces an opportunity to demonstrate that institutions can and in fact do bring people and countries together around practical cooperation and shared solutions. We nominated Ms. Fernanda Espinosa in the conviction that her expertise, experience, and diplomatic leadership and commitment to the multilateral system can help to strengthen the United Nations, restore confidence in its institutions, and ensure that the multilateral system delivers to all Member States, large and small. These are not separate initiatives. Do not see me as diverting from the course of our discussions. See it within the context of rebuilding trust, of rebuilding institutions required to ensure that the legal processes, accompanying legal processes, are foolproof and respected. These are not, like I said, separate initiatives. They reflect a common assertion that the answer to the shortcomings of multilateralism is not to withdraw in insularity, but to collaborate to shape the multilateralism that is more accountable, more representative, and more effective, and better able to deliver. For Antigua and Barbuda, there is simply too much at stake to accept a world where power alone determines outcomes. We will continue to use every platform available to us, whether here at the United Nations, at the Commonwealth, or regional international institutions, to help maintain, repair, and strengthen that order. Because for countries like mine, multilateralism and the preservation of a global order, they're not optional. They are just how we ensure that the international system works and works for everyone, if it pleases you. Thank you.

I thank Mr. Green for his remarks.

Thank you very much, Oman. We now go to Iran. His Excellency, Mr. Kazem Gharib-Abad.

Bismillahirrahmanirrahim. Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, it's a pleasure to be here today at this meeting on the defense of international law, convened at the initiative of our two friendly countries, Malaysia and South Africa. The Islamic Republic of Iran firmly believes that international law, if it is truly to serve as a guardian of peace, justice and human dignity, cannot become a collection of selective rules that are rigorously enforced against some states while being disregarded in the case of others due to political considerations and power. The credibility of international law rests on the equality of states before the law, not on equality before power. The Charter of the United Nations has established the prohibition of the use of force, respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states. the peaceful settlement of disputes, and the protection of the fundamental rights of peoples as pillars of the post-World War II international order. Yet today, more than ever, we face a fundamental question. Are the rules of international law truly applied equally to all? If the answer is yes, the international community must demonstrate this principle in practice. Palestine today represents one of the clearest tests of the credibility of the international legal order. Decades of occupation, settlement expansion, the denial of the rights of the Palestinian people, and their deprivation on the right to self-determination, followed by the devastating humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, have demonstrated how wide the gap can become between the rules of international law and their implementation. The Islamic Republic of Iran believes that the Palestinian people, like all peoples, possess rights that cannot be made conditional upon political considerations, alliances, or geopolitical calculations. The right to self-determination, the protection of civilians, and the prohibition of collective punishment are not principles that can be subject to political negotiation. International law is either universal or it becomes in practice an instrument of discrimination. In this context, the decision by the Republic of South Africa to bring proceedings before the International Court of Justice concerning the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in relation to Gaza is of particular significance. In January 2024, at the provisional measures stage, the Court indicated measures aimed at protecting the rights claimed by the Palestinians under the Genocide Convention. The case remains before the Court, and judicial proceedings have continued in 2026. The significance of this process lies not only in the eventual outcome of a judicial case, but also in the fact that a state relying on available multilateral legal mechanisms has sought to place the principles of accountability and responsibility for the suffering of a people before an international judicial institution. This is precisely the path that the international system must strengthen. Less impunity, more accountability. Less political power above the law and more law above power. Ladies and gentlemen, Iran too has in past 16 months face blatant violations of the fundamental principles of the Charter. On 28 February 2026, a new round of military aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran began, in the context of what became a 40-day war. Only at the first day of the war the Supreme Leader of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and 168 students and teachers at an elementary school in the city of Minab were martyred. The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is clear. The sovereignty and territorial integrity of a state cannot be violated or made subject to political bargaining. No state can merely on the basis of political assertions or the unilateral interpretation of a perceived threat set aside the fundamental prohibition on the use of force. If the fundamental principle enshrined in Article 2, paragraph 4 of the United Nations Charter is weakened, no country, large or small, can have confidence in its security and sovereignty. Iran also maintains that when confronted with an armed attack, The right of self-defense within the framework of the charter and international law is a legitimate and lawful right of the victim state. At the same time, the Islamic Republic of Iran emphasizes the obligation to respect international humanitarian law, protect civilians, and distinguish between military objectives and civilian objects. These principles must be respected without expansion. exception, whether in Palestine, Iran, Lebanon or anywhere else in the world, the fundamental problem today is not the absence of rules of international law. The problem is their selective application. In one crisis, the Charter is invoked. In another, geopolitical interests take precedence over the Charter. In one case, Security Council resolutions are vigorously demanded. In another, years of violations of resolutions remain without effective action. In one situation, investigations and accountability are demanded. In another, political protection stands in the way of accountability. Such an approach not only undermines justice, it also erodes the confidence of peoples in multilateralism and international institutions. If international law is not applied equally to the powerful and the weak, to allies and non-allies, to East and West, and to the global North and global South, its credibility will continue to erode. From this perspective, the role of International Court of Justice assumes even greater importance. The court must be able, as the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, to adjudicate disputes between states independently of political pressure and to clarify the legal obligations of the states. South Africa's action in the Palestine case is an important example of the use of the judicial mechanisms available within the international system. It is also important to note that in August 2026, South Africa submitted to the court a dossier concerning non-compliance with the provisional measures indicated by the Court. This process carries an important message. The issuance of a judgment or a judicial order is not the end of the road. Its implementation is an integral part of international justice. If decisions of international judicial institutions are not implemented, it is not only the rights of the victims that suffer, the credibility of the international legal order itself is also undermined. Exorcist, the Islamic Republic of Iran believes that today's meeting must go beyond expressing concerns. We need a set of practical measures. First, unconditional and non-discriminatory respect for the Charter of the United Nations and the prohibition of the use of force. Second, ensuring the effective implementation of the decisions and orders of the International Court of Justice. Third, ending impunity of serious violations of international criminal offenses and international humanitarian law. Fourth, supporting the right of nations to self-determination including the Palestinian people. Fifth, strengthening the role of the countries of the global south in shaping a fairer international order and ensuring more genuine representation in multilateral institutions. And sixth, reforming the structures that enable the selective application of international law. Ladies and gentlemen, the world today stands at a crossroads. We can witness the gradual erosion of the rules that the international community has developed over decades to prevent war, aggression, occupation, and atrocities, or we can choose to restore international law as the common standard governing the conduct of the states. Palestine, Iran, and many other situations have shown us that this is no longer a theoretical choice. It's a choice about human lives. It's a choice about the sovereign of a state. It's a choice about the right of peoples to self-determination. And it's a choice about the future of the multilateral system at the heart of which stands the United Nations. The Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready to work with all the states committed to sovereign equality, multilateralism, the peaceful settlement of disputes and the non-discriminatory implementation of international law in order to strengthen this system. Let us not allow law to become subordinate to power. Let us ensure that power remains subject to law. I thank Malaysia and South Africa for convening this important meeting and for their continued efforts the defense of multilateralism and international law. I thank you.

Thank you very much, my dear brother, Minister Mario Vieira, for your input. We now go to Cabo Verde.

Thank you very much, Cabo Verde, for your input. We now go to Cuba. His Excellency, Mr. Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Cuba.

Were the US government allowed to destroy a small nation with the aim of changing its political system? or with any other design in mind, the world would become even more dangerous than it is already. What would happen afterwards? Who would be the next victim? That's what we could ask ourselves. We thank the member states of the Hague group for their statements in favor of lifting the blockade and the energy barrier against Cuba and the numerous expressions of support and solidarity towards our country from the peoples of the world. Cuba is a country of peace. We are not a threat to anyone. We are right. We are on the side of justice. We will continue defending ourselves, cost us what it may. as we have a right to freedom of determination and nothing will take us away from our socialist development project that we are moving forward with, which is what our people freely chose. Thank you very much.
Thank you, Your Excellency, for your input. We now go to take Mr. Musa Kula Kikaya. The Deputy Foreign Minister of Turkey, you now have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chairperson. And also, I would like to thank co-organizers of this valuable meeting. Excellencies, esteemed participants, I would like to begin by thanking the HEU Group for organizing this meeting in support of Palestinian rights. Turkiye supports any efforts towards fair and lasting settlement of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Israel continues to disregard international legal order, which perpetuates chaos and instabilities in regional and global scans. The war against Iran has worsened the stability and economic balance in the entire Middle East and beyond. Palestine faces multiple challenges. As part of Israel's genocidal policies in Gaza, civilian infrastructure was razed. Civilian population was forcefully displaced. International aid organizations, including even a UN agency, UNRWA, was deliberately targeted. Furthermore, settler colonialism continues to entrench in the West Bank. The state-sponsored settler terrorism aims at ethnic cleansing. The current path that the Netanyahu government has chosen requires a collective and concerted international effort to prevent further undermining of international law. It is time to turn our tireless efforts into concrete actions against Israel. Those actions may include arms embargo, isolation of Israel within the international community, recognition of State of Palestine and ensuring its UN membership, awareness in public opinions, making accountable Israel for the crimes committed. Turkiye is in the forefront of the sanctions against Israel. We have entirely stopped bilateral trade with Israel, which amounted to $10 billion in 2022. We have submitted our declaration of intervention before the International Court of Justice for the case brought by South Africa. We closed our ports to Israeli ships. Turkish port authorities require shipping agents to provide letters declaring that vessels are not linked to Israel and not carrying military or hazardous cargo bound for Israel. Dear colleagues, we also face significant challenges in our continued support for the Palestinian cause. It's essential to reflect on how domestic electoral shifts within a nation can lead to a fundamental change of its foreign policy, regarding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In the current global landscape, our primary objective must be to ensure that the Palestinian issue remains a unifying principle rather than a source of domestic or international polarization. In this context, the advisory opinions of the ICJ should guide every country. We reaffirm our unwavering commitment to implementing coordinated diplomatic and legal measures in defense of international law, pursuing comprehensive accountability, and maintaining solidarity with the people of Palestine. Turkey remains committed to the two-state solution as the only viable path toward lasting peace. We will persist on our path for justice and peace. I thank you.
Thank you, Tekir. We now go to Mexico. You now have the floor.

Mr. Chair. Mexico takes note with appreciation of the convening of this timely meeting on the defense of international law by Malaysia and South Africa. Mexico reaffirms its commitment to the defense of international law, multilateralism, and the principles of the Charter of the UN, enshrined in our national constitution as a guiding principles or foreign policy and as a compass of our national international projects. The Chairman, the challenge before us is to preserve the continued relevance of the purposes and principles of the Charter as the best possible international legal framework for the maintenance of international peace and security, the promotion of sustainable development, and the protection of human rights. while ensuring that our international legal system remains capable of responding to contemporary realities and challenges. We must ensure and enhance compliance with an implementation of international law that has been mentioned before by the previous persons that spoke before me, in particularly on the question of Palestine, Mexico supports the two-state solution. In this context, Mexico reiterates its continued support for the institutions entrusted with giving effect to these principles, in particular the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court, the latter today under strain. Both played a fundamental role in strengthening the rule of law at the international level in the interpretation and application of international law and in the fight against impunity for the most heinous crimes. and the contents of international law to whether with implementation we should continue the progressive development of international law and to continue to clarify the interpretation of an application of the charter, in particular of Article 51 of that instrument. We call to the attention and support for the proposal made by my delegation in the Charter Committee on the important issue to the maintenance of international peace and security and whose work is relevant to this Hague group. The strength and legitimacy of international order would be measured by its ability to protect people, respond to the challenges, and ensure the law is an effective means of peace, justice, and human dignity. Mexico will continue to follow closely the initiative, particularly as it enters this new phase. Thank you very much for your attention.
Thank you very much, Mexico. We now go to Indonesia.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, Excellencies. On behalf of Foreign Minister Sugiono, I would like to thank South Africa and Malaysia for convening this important meeting. We meet at a time when international law is increasingly challenged and when opposition to its applications is sometimes expressed openly. For Indonesia, this is precisely why the work of this group matters. Indonesia supports the implementation of the ICJ advisory opinion on the legal consequences arising from Israel's policies and practices in the occupied Palestinian territory. The law is clear. Our challenge now is to give it practical consequence. Indonesia has taken concrete steps in this direction, as reflected in the UN Secretary-General's report on the implementation of Resolution ES-10/24. Excellencies, Indonesia has long held this principled position. We do not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel for as long as Palestine remains under occupation. We remain committed to ensuring that Indonesian nationals, companies, and entities under our jurisdictions do not contribute to recognition of or support for Israel's illegal presence in occupied Palestinian territory. We have also joined calls to halt arms transfers where there is a risk of contributing to violation of international law. At the same time, we continue to support Palestinian economic self-determination, including through preferential market access for Palestinian products. Since 2018, imports of Palestinian dates have increased by more than 130 percent, and we are working to expand the scheme to additional Palestinian products. Excellencies, the broader question before us is: how do we expand the work of this group beyond its membership? We must be able to turn legal clarity into broader state practice. Therefore, group must offer a practical pathway for state to act for instance could we consider a simple voluntary mechanism for state to share what steps they have taken to implement the ICJ advisory opinion and the solution es10/24 this would allow us to identify not only progress but also practical obstacles and help overcome them perhaps this is where the groups could contribute by helping states translate international law into consistent national practice. In this regard, Indonesia stands ready to work toward this objective. I thank you.
Thank you, Indonesia, for your input. We will now have Varsha Kandikoda, the Executive Secretary of the Hague Group, to give us a summary of our discussions and the next steps.

Thank you, Minister Lamulla. Greetings to the co-chairs, South Africa, our co-sponsor, Malaysia, our distinguished experts today, William Schabas and Deanna Buttu, and with gratitude to special remarks from Palestine, Norway, Maldives, and Brazil. I thank all the countries present here today, especially the foreign ministers and ministers of justice who have traveled to this meeting. Today's meeting of 40 states began with a very clear conviction that is on each of your tables in front of you, that the authority of international law derives not merely from its proclamation, but from its enforcement. We reaffirm the Charter of the United Nations, as declared by every delegate on this floor, to ensure that the rights it affirms for all peoples are not merely declared but defended. Again, as every delegate on this floor has warned, the alternative is a world in which might alone determines which laws are respected and which may be violated with impunity. Today's meeting represents the largest meeting convened by the Hague Group so far, with over 40 member states participating in this extraordinary gathering in defense of international law. Growing from a fledgling platform of nine member states a little over a year ago to 31 states in Bogota in Colombia, 35 states meeting in New York on the sidelines of last year's UN General Assembly, to nearly 40 states inside today's historic trusteeship council chamber. through every speech on this floor, I'd like to identify three key levers of shifts, desires that have been demanded by member states present here today. The first is from complicity to compliance. Today, states commit to cooperation and exchange across national and international mechanisms to give practical effect to states' obligations under international law and the determinations made by international judicial bodies. This includes The continuation of efforts aimed at obtaining a United Nations Security Council arms embargo as put forth by Maldives, Turkey, Indonesia, to target settlement products as proposed by the delegate from Indonesia. And here I'd like to acknowledge the work and the recent legislations by our member states who are present in the room today who are observer states, Spain and the United Kingdom. Accountability in business practices, as proposed by the delegate from Norway, to ensure that our industry, our territorial waters, ships, vessels, and ports do not serve as conduits for activities that enable or facilitate genocide, war crimes, or crimes against humanity. The second shift that we heard from speeches across the floor today is a shift from impunity to accountability. Today, states have committed once again to strengthening the defense and independence of the international legal order. Accountability for settlers, officials promoting settlements, mass confinement, and violence against Palestinians, as put forth by the Minister from Brazil. Coordinated measures to support the implementation and enforcement of the decisions of the international courts and tribunals, as proposed by Oman, Qatar, Cabo Verde. to oppose the efforts to obstruct, undermine, and retaliate against their work, against officials of the courts of UN special rapporteurs, through measures such as blocking statutes, as proposed by the co-sponsors of today's meeting, and through sustained financial support to organizations like UNDRR, as proposed by Palestine. Through both of these two key levers and shifts, we see a desire for a much larger, broader, paradigmatic shift towards a new, multilateralism, to reaffirm the sovereign equality of nations large and small, and strengthening international cooperation in the maintenance of international peace and security. We have once again heard a call for a renewed United Nations body modeled after the historic 1962 UN Special Committee Against Apartheid, as proposed by several member states today on this floor. As declared by delegates from Iran to Indonesia, Mexico to Brazil, and in the words of the foreign minister of Antigua and Barbuda, we know that the preservation of multilateralism is not optional. Your Excellencies, I thank you all again for your continued engagement with the Hague Group, with your national policies, and for the defense of international law. From Palestine to Lebanon, Cuba to Sudan, the defense of humanity is our common cause. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much for the summary that you have provided to us. We are very thankful and it does give us a clear way forward for all the participants. I will now read the closing remarks for our meeting. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I thank you for the richness of this discussion, and in particular for the concrete proposals that have been placed before us. As we have heard in the summary of our discussions, there is considerable scope for States to work together to defend international legal order and to translate our existing obligations into practical actions. What we have heard today will inform the core sponsor statements to be issued by South Africa and Malaysia following this meeting, reflecting the interventions of the participating States and the concrete proposal advanced during our discussions. The central message of today's meeting is clear: international law cannot defend itself. Its authority ultimately depends upon States being prepared to uphold it consistently, to implement the obligations they have accepted and to defend the institutions entrusted with applying it. The authority of international law derives not merely from its proclamation, but from its enforcement. The alternative is a world in which might alone determines which laws are respected and which may be violated with impunity. The defense of international law is therefore not the responsibility of one member state, one region, or one institution. It's a common and a shared responsibility. The defense of humanity is our common cause. States must work together to ensure that the obligations we have collectively established are implemented consistently and effectively. I thank Malaysia for co-sponsoring today's meeting. And I thank all participating States, international organizations, United Nations representatives, and our experts who graced us with their occasions and made meaningful inputs for all our engagements. I also thank the United Nations Secretariat and all those who have worked to make this meeting possible. This concludes the formal proceedings of the High-Level Meeting in Defense of International Law. I thank all of you. Our meeting is now adjourned. Thank you very much. Thank you. Thank you. You too. But.
